title: Power outages and generators: the cost to developing economies

Power outages, generators, and firm performance

Joshua Wimpey

Phoebe Ishak

November 20, 2026

This page in:

For many African businesses, generators are not backup but a second power system - and a routine cost of doing business. | © Shutterstock.com

Unreliable electricity is one of the most expensive constraints on businesses in the developing world. It does not arrive as a crisis. It arrives as a routine: machines and refrigerators stop, the payment terminal goes dark, and the working day is quietly shortened. Drawing on 292,581 firm interviews across 186 economies from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys (2005-2025), this post asks two questions. How large is the cost of outages? And how far does buying a generator go in offsetting it?

A burden that falls on a handful of regions
Across all surveyed economies, 52 percent of firms experienced power outages in the last fiscal year, and 47 percent describe electricity as an obstacle to their operations. These averages hide extraordinary concentration. In Sub-Saharan Africa, 75 percent of firms report outages, averaging close to 8 a month, and costing an average of 5.2 percent of annual sales. In high-income OECD economies, the figures are 27 percent, 0.3 outages per month, and 0.2 percent of sales. The Middle East and North Africa and South Asia sit in between on incidence but at the top on frequency rankings, at roughly 13 to 16 outages a month.

Figure 1. Incidence, frequency and cost of power outages by region. World Bank Enterprise Surveys, 2005–2025.

Three bar charts comparing seven regions. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest share of firms reporting power outages (74 percent) and the largest sales losses (5.2 percent of annual sales). South Asia has the most outages in a typical month (16.9), followed by the Middle East and North Africa (10.7). High-income OECD economies have the fewest outages and losses on every measure.

Where the grid fails, firms build their own
Roughly 30 percent of firms own or share a generator, rising to 42 percent among firms that experience outages. Among users, generators supply about a fifth of electricity consumption on average, and more than 70 percent for the top decile. For these firms, the generator is not a backup. It is a parallel power system and a standard cost of doing business.

Figure 2. Generator ownership rises with outage frequency. Most recent survey per economy with at least 50 firms surveyed.

Scatter chart of 182 economies: power outages in a typical month against the share of firms owning or sharing a generator. Generator use rises with outages (correlation 0.46). Many Sub-Saharan African economies, such as Nigeria, Chad and Ghana, combine frequent outages with generator ownership above 65 percent. Economies with almost no outages, such as Japan and Singapore, have low generator use.

What changes when a firm buys a generator?
We followed more than 18,000 establishments across multiple survey waves (39,000 total observations), comparing firms that switched to owning a generator with firms that never own one, and controlling for firm and survey-wave fixed effects.

Figure 3. Difference-in-differences estimates of generator adoption on firm outcomes. Comparison group: firms that never owned a generator.

Dot plot of difference-in-differences estimates with 95 percent confidence intervals for five firm outcomes after buying a generator. Sales rise by 0.267, employment by 0.149, fixed-asset investment by 0.050 and sales lost to outages by 0.080; firm exit falls by 0.027. All confidence intervals exclude zero.

Sales, employment and outage losses are in logs; investment and exit are shares.

After adoption, sales were about 31 percent and employment by about 16 percent relative to non-adopters, implying labor productivity gains of about 12 percent. Adopters are 5 percentage points more likely to invest in fixed assets and exit between survey waves falls by 2.7 percentage points from a base rate of 3 percent. Two caveats apply. Firms must survive long enough to report adopting a generator, which mechanically lowers measured exit among adopters. And firms may buy generators when they are already expanding. These results are best read as strong associations rather than precise causal effects.
However, adopting a generator does not reduce reported sales losses from outages, and adopters become more likely to call electricity an obstacle (+4.7 percentage points). Several explanations are plausible, including:

Timing: firms buy generators when grid supply is deteriorating.

Imperfect substitution: generators carry fuel costs and switching delays, and processes such as cold chains, continuous manufacturing, and payment systems are damaged by the interruption itself.

Measurement: lost sales are self-reported, and owning a generator may make firms more aware of outages or change how they estimate losses.

Generator ownership is a privilege, not ever firm can afford to self-insure
Generators are far from equally accessible. In the third of economies with the most frequent outages, 76 percent of large firms own or share a generator, compared with 40 percent of small firms. Elsewhere, the gap persists at lower levels: 41 percent versus 15 percent.

Finance also plays a role. In the most outage-prone economies, firms with a bank loan or line of credit are more likely to own a generator at every size: 47 percent versus 39 percent among small firms, 64 versus 59 percent among medium firms, and 81 versus 71 percent among large ones. A generator requires a lumpy, up-front investment with an ongoing fuel bill, so firms that struggle to borrow are less able to protect themselves. Credit constraints and infrastructure failures compound each other.

What does this mean for policy?

Grid reliability is not just energy policy; it is business policy.  Reliable power is closely tied to firm growth and survival. Utility performance should be judged by what reliability it delivers for businesses, not only by generation capacity targets.

High generator ownership is not a sign of successful adaptation. It measures the depth of infrastructure failure and represents a costly, carbon-intensive duplication of capital that the grid was supposed to provide.

Where reliability cannot improve quickly, make coping affordable. Better access to credit and alternatives to diesel could help narrow a gap that affects firm survival. Banks and utility providers may find solutions in financing firm-level energy and storage investments that benefit both firms and utilities through improved grid reliability.

Measure the right thing. Lost sales from outages persist after generator purchase, making them a poor measure of electricity as a constraint. Survival, employment, and investment tell the story more accurately.

The bottom line
In Sub-Saharan Africa, power outages cost firms around 5 percent of annual sales, more than 25 times the burden in high-income economies. Generators appear to help firms grow, invest and survive, but they do not eliminate losses related to power outages: they offset part of the damage, at a cost only some firms can afford. Firms that can afford a generator pull ahead, while small and credit-constrained firms fall behind.
